column2: With the snowplow {C3}(a ski braking technique){C0} I had finally learned, I somehow made it down to the rest house at the foot of the mountain and took a breath.
Right in front of me, {n2} stopped gracefully in a spray of snow.
My goggles were plastered with powder snow, and I couldn't see a thing.
“Ha ha,
{n1}, you look like a snowman.”
I heard {n2} laughing.
I took off my goggles and brushed the snow off my body.
I took off my goggles and brushed the snow off my body.
“Fine, I look better rolling than skiing anyway.”
“That's not what I meant!
I think you're improving fast.”
{n2} took off her goggles too and flashed a smile.
After hours, seeing that smile was like seeing the sun peek out from behind the clouds.
I looked at {n2} again.
Her long black hair stood out beautifully against her white ski wear.
She glided down even the toughest slopes with ease and had been the center of attention on the runs.
I'm sure everyone had hoped for a beautiful face under that pair of goggles.
That's just how ski resorts are.
If it was {n2},
I thought, she'd surely disappoint no one's expectations.
All day I'd been fed up with {n2}, a girl raised in snow country, showing off how much better she was than me, but just then I felt proud.
I knew not only her face but also how attractive the figure hidden under that thick ski wear was.
“Let's do just one more run, okay?”
“What?
Still skiing?”
I asked back, exhausted.
After a day of brutal training since morning, I could barely stand.
“Come on.
Please?
Just one more.”
{n2} pressed her palms together as if praying.
“Let's go back already.
Besides, look, the weather's looking dicey.”
I pointed at the sky.
It was no lie.
The sun, which had been drifting in and out from behind the clouds, had vanished completely.
The whole sky felt black and heavy, pressing down on us.
“You're right.
It might blizzard tonight.”
{n2} furrowed her brow.
“...Then let's head back for today.”
We climbed into the four-wheel drive we'd borrowed from {n2}'s uncle, Mr. Kobayashi.
I had met {n2} at college this past April.
It was this fall that my bold, relentless advances finally got us to the point of going on a few dates.
But no matter how hard I pushed, I got no response, and it had started to feel like a one-man sumo match.
So when she herself invited me to go skiing together, I honestly was surprised.
Her uncle, a man named Jiro Kobayashi, runs an inn in Shinano {C3}(now Nagano){C0}.
But it's a bit far from the slopes and inconvenient, so apparently it doesn't get many guests even in season.
So {n2} invited me, since we could stay at a bargain price.
I gladly said yes, and yesterday, that is,
December 21, I had arrived here in Shinano.
By the time we got back to the inn, the sun had set completely and snow had begun to fall.
The “Spur,” run by the Kobayashis, was a stylish inn with a log cabin exterior and an interior done mostly in white.
The menu was international, or maybe borderless, but in any case wonderfully varied, and every dish was satisfying besides.
Far from empty, it seemed to have been featured in magazines and was growing popular.
Because we're not busy, a bargain...
I realized after arriving yesterday that Mr. Kobayashi had said that so we wouldn't feel obliged.
Unfortunately, or perhaps naturally, {n2} and I had separate rooms.
We...
We...
Change, then meet in the lounge.
Sofas were arranged around a large brown table.
We decided to sit there and wait until dinner started.
Just as we sat down, we heard girls' voices chattering from the second floor.
They looked like office workers, probably the same age as us or a year or two younger.
The three came down the stairs, talking among themselves.
“I never thought it'd be this far from the slopes.”
That was the thin girl with long hair.
Her eyes were a bit sharp, but she was pretty enough.
She gave a frivolous impression.
“...But it says right here the food is great, remember?”
The girl who pointed at a page of the rolled-up guidebook with the pen in her right hand had a figure that said she cared more about eating than skiing.
Even now she was eating snacks alone, clutching a bag under her arm.
She seemed a bit overweight, but with a panda-like charm.
“That's why I didn't want to leave it up to Keiko!
If you want good food, Tokyo has plenty, doesn't it?{r}{p}Honestly...”
The long-haired girl fumed.
“Now, now.{r}{p}Come on.
The atmosphere isn't bad either.{r}{p}Places like this probably have better service.”
The one trying to calm her down was the third girl, who wore glasses.
Her boyish short hair suited her round glasses well.
She looked like the most capable of the three.
“Which one do you like?”
{n2} whispered in a cold voice.
what are you saying?! I...”
I flustered.
With {n2} right next to me, there was no way my eyes would wander to other girls.
But I was too embarrassed to say so.
“Excuse me.
Could you take a picture for us?”
One of the trio, the girl with glasses, approached us holding out her camera.
She probably asked me because I'm a guy.
“Huh?
...Sure, no problem.”
The camera was the autofocus type, with an automatic flash.
I accepted easily.
But still...
...I had always hated that “Say cheese!” thing.
I can't understand the nerve of people who say such a stupid line without flinching.
I suppose the reason is that it makes you smile.
But if the shutter clicks right on the “ch,” everyone ends up looking like they're sucking a lemon.
If they have to say something, “kiwi” or “bikini” would be better...
That's what I secretly think, but it's embarrassing anyway, so I've never told anyone.
...Without letting any of that show, I looked through the viewfinder.
The three girls huddled together and smiled.
“Ready?”
I pressed the shutter.
“Thank you very much.”
The girls bowed their heads as they took the camera back.
It would be odd to stay silent, so we introduced ourselves.
The long-haired one, who'd been grumbling about the distance from the slopes, was Kanako Watase.
The plump, cute one still eating snacks was Keiko Kitano.
And the one with glasses holding the camera was Aki Kawamura.
All three were eighteen-year-old office workers, apparently.
“We just got here, but how are the slopes?”
Kanako asked me.
But since it was my first time, there was no way I could say whether they were good or bad.
{n2} answered for me.
“Pretty good.{r}{p}The lifts aren't that crowded.”
Kanako seemed as keen on skiing as {n2}, and they quickly got into talk about snow quality and which runs were great.
The other two listened with a somewhat cooled-off air.
Maybe Kanako had dragged them along by force.
Just then an engine approached and stopped in front of the inn.
It seemed a new guest had arrived.
After a while, along with the sound of the bell on the front door, a loud voice in Osaka dialect rang out.
“Whew, saved!
Thought I was gonna die.”
A man and a woman came in, snow piled on the shoulders and heads of their coats.
A plump, red-faced man just under fifty and a slender, tall woman who looked to be in her late thirties.
“Ah, Mr. Kayama, welcome.{r}{p}You're late.
We were worried.”
Mr. Kobayashi came out from the back to greet the couple.
“Blizzard started up real sudden-like, nearly got lost.”
Looking out the window, I saw the snow, which hadn't been that bad earlier, picking up strength by the minute.
The old-fashioned cuckoo clock on the wall struck seven.
I reflexively looked at my digital watch, but it still said 18:55.
Maybe the clock was fast.
“Dinner is ready, so please come to the dining room.”
Midori Shinozaki, the part-timer, came out of the dining room.
“We'll carry up your bags and coats, so please go on to the dining room, Mr. Kayama.”
At the front desk, Mr. Kobayashi was urging the couple, who had finished signing in, to have dinner.
I happened to be looking over there, and my eyes met the wife's.
Her eyes looked sad...
The feeling lasted only a moment.
She smiled and gave a slight bow.
I hurriedly returned it.
When I noticed, {n2} was looking at her too.
I thought she might tease me again, but contrary to my expectation, she murmured:
“She's pretty.”
“...Yeah.”
I answered honestly.
{n2} fixed me with a serious gaze and asked:
“Do you think a fragile, blow-away type like that is more feminine?”
“...Well, yeah, kind of...
Oh, but you have your feminine side too, {n2}.”
“'Too'?
What do you mean, 'too'?{r}{p}How rude.”
I had chosen my words badly.
{n2} turned her face away with a huff, stood up quickly, and headed toward the dining room.
I hurried after her.
The dining room tables were already set with knives and forks.
The three girls and the couple who had just arrived were already seated.
I sat at the table where {n2} had briskly taken her seat.
In the middle of the table stood a candle shaped like a Christmas tree.
Its flickering little flame lit the profile of {n2}, gazing out the window, with a faint red glow.
“Beautiful.”...Smooth, like an actor.
“Beautiful.”...{g}
I played it smooth, like an actor in a foreign film...{p}or I would have, but there was no way I could say a line like that.{g}
I just gazed at her.{g}
“What are you looking at?{g}
Staring blankly like that.{r}{p}Are you that hungry?”{g}
...Oh well.{g}
Mr. Kobayashi's wife Kyoko and the part-timer Midori carried the dishes to each table.
The guests were us, the three girls, and the couple who arrived late...
or so I thought, but there was one more guest who looked out of place at an inn like this.
A man in a coat, sitting in a corner of the dining room as if blending into the wall.
He hadn't taken off his jacket or hat even at dinner, and was even wearing black sunglasses.
He certainly didn't look like a skier, or even a salesman here on business.
...Yakuza.
My first impression.
...Yakuza.
My first impression.
“A yakuza, here...?”
I blurted.
But thinking about it, I couldn't imagine a yakuza coming to an inn alone.
Watching him quietly sip his soup, I began to think he might be a nice guy despite his looks.
Maybe he kept his sunglasses on simply out of shyness, or maybe they were prescription and he planned to go skiing in them.
Either way, once our food arrived, none of that mattered anymore.
“Delicious!”
{n2} gasped after her first spoonful of soup.
It was an Italian dish called minestrone, full of small diced vegetables.
The piping hot soup was truly delicious and warmed me from the inside.
The dishes that followed were all satisfying in both taste and quantity, and sighs of contentment came from all around.
I thought again that this place could make it as a restaurant, not just an inn.
In fact, that yakuza-looking man and the middle-aged couple might have come just for the food.
“Does your aunt make all this?”
I asked {n2} over after-dinner coffee.
“I think my aunt just helps out.{r}{p}My uncle's the one who loves cooking.{r}{p}He's wanted to be a chef since he was a kid.”
“Huh.”
“He gave it up and became a salaryman for a while, but he couldn't let go of the dream.{r}{p}They didn't have kids either, so he quit the corporate world and started an inn.”
“...That must be tough.”
I was impressed.
“I'm sure it is.
But as it happens, my grandfather, my mother's father, that is...”
“Yeah.”
“Grandfather owned several mountains around here.{r}{p}They had the land from the start, so it seems they didn't struggle much on that front.”
So {n2}'s family
is super rich.”
I felt a bit intimidated.
“Not at all.
Most of the land went to my uncle, the eldest son.{r}{p}We're just ordinary salarymen.{r}{p}And our house is tiny.”
Thank goodness it wasn't a love across social classes...
People who had finished eating trickled out of the dining room in twos and threes.
My digital watch read 19:55.
“Well then.
Shall we go night skiing?”
{n2} said something unbelievable and stood up.
“Y-you're kidding,
night skiing in this blizzard?”
My body was shredded already.
“Going by the weather report, forget night skiing.”
Midori, in her apron, cut in from the side.
“Looks safest not to go out for a while.”
Midori Shinozaki, the part-timer, was of indeterminate age.
I figured she was probably in her twenties, but sometimes she looked like a high schooler and sometimes like a middle-aged lady.
Maybe she spent all her free time on the slopes; her face and hair were so sun-and-snow-tanned she looked like a surfer.
“Is it that bad?”
I was half relieved and half worried.
“The forecast says it could be the heaviest snow in years.”
This time the other part-timer, Toshio Kubota, came over.
Toshio called himself a sixth-year college student.
He loved skiing so much that he kept this part-time job and neglected his credits, apparently.
He stood well over 180 centimeters, and with his build he looked like an all-around athlete, skiing and everything.
His tan was a close match for Midori's.
...In front of someone like that, I somehow feel intimidated.
Especially if I'm with my girlfriend...
I checked {n2}'s reaction.
Her eyes weren't sparkling with admiration, and she showed no sign of a racing heart.
...Relief.
“We won't get snowed in here and starve to death, will we?”
When I asked, Toshio waved a hand and laughed.
“No worries.
We're far from town, so we always keep plenty of food. Counting canned goods, we could feed this many people their fill for three weeks.”
Being stuck for three weeks was a chilling thought.
...Then again, being stuck with {n2} might not be so bad.
With that thought, I glanced at her.
“Hm?
What is it?”
“N-nothing.”
Toshio said, sounding genuinely sorry.
“Three weeks is an exaggeration, but skiing tomorrow might be out. Well, school's on break, so a day or two extra won't matter, right?”
“Hmm...
depends on Uncle.{r}{p}Given the circumstances, he might let us stay extra.{r}{p}Right,
{n1}, you're fine with that, aren't you?”
“Huh?
...Oh, sure.”
I smiled back.
I actually had a part-time job, but this was a rare opportunity, so I could turn it down.
Something good might happen while we spend a few days here...
While I was lost in such thoughts, a commotion drifted from the hall.
{n2} and I heaved ourselves up and left the dining room.
Near the front desk, the three girls were shouting something at Mr. Kobayashi.
“Now, now.
Please calm down and tell me.{r}{p}What on earth happened?”
“That's what I'm saying!
We just got back to our room, and on the floor there was this...
this...!”
The girls, trembling, held out a small scrap of paper to Mr. Kobayashi.
Peeking in from the side, I saw characters scrawled with something like a red marker.
'Tonight,
12 o'clock,
someone
will die'
“Tonight,
12 o'clock,
someone
...will die?!”
When I read it aloud, everyone gasped in unison.
A few seconds later, Mr. Kobayashi finally spoke.
“Must be somebody's prank.”
“...In poor taste.”
{n2} frowned.
It was indeed a tasteless prank.
If it really was a prank, that is...
“But somebody came into our room and left this, you know? It's creepy, I can't sleep in there.”
Kanako's face twisted as if she were about to cry.
“If it was on the floor, couldn't someone have slid it in through the gap under the door?{r}{p}You did lock it, didn't you?”
At Mr. Kobayashi's words, the girls looked blank.
“Oh, I see,
they didn't have to come in.”
Apparently that hadn't even occurred to them.
“...But it's still creepy.”
That was Aki, the one with glasses.
“Would you like to switch rooms?{r}{p}Luckily we have vacancies.”
“Does that room have a TV too?”
When Keiko asked, Mr. Kobayashi shook his head apologetically.
“I'm sorry.
Our guest rooms generally don't have TVs.{r}{p}Only two rooms do, and those are the ones you're in now.”
“What about the other one?”
“Unfortunately it's occupied.{r}{p}So if you want to watch TV, you'll have to put up with your current room...”
“What should we do?”
The three looked at each other and began to discuss.
“I still think it's creepy.”
That was Aki.
“Should we do without TV?”
Kanako answered.
“Aw,
there's a show I want to watch.”
Keiko started being selfish.
“Forget TV!
What did you come here for?{r}{p}We came to ski, to ski!”
Kanako began to get angry.
“I know, but...
I can't miss it today.{r}{p}It's the finale of 'Jackpot.'”
I'd never seen it, but I think it was a gambling drama called 'Jackpot in London.'
In the end, since it was a pointless prank and switching rooms didn't seem to accomplish much, they withdrew to their rooms.
“But who would pull a prank like this?{r}{p}There aren't any kids staying here...”
{n2} turned a mischievous look on me.
“Could it have been you, {n1}?”
She said the most outrageous thing.
Mr. Kobayashi looked at me in surprise too.
“Not a chance.
Why would I do that to girls I barely know?”
I protested in shock.
“Right.
Not even you would do something like this, {n1}.”
Something about that phrasing bothered me, but I let it go.
Just then the phone at the front desk started to ring.
Hello,
this is 'Spur.'”
Half listening to Mr. Kobayashi talk, we sat on the sofa in the empty lounge.
Mr. Kobayashi's loud voice carried easily to where we sat.
“Ah, Mr. Mikimoto.{r}{p}Dinner has finished, I'm afraid, but your room is reserved.{r}{p}...Yes
...yes
...near the station? From there it would take thirty or forty minutes by car, I think, and the snow's gotten quite bad now, so...”
“Looks like someone's coming this late.{r}{p}Maybe snow delayed him.”
{n2} whispered.
“Probably.
Hope he doesn't get lost and stranded.”
“...I see.
Then we'll be waiting for you.”
Just as Mr. Kobayashi finished his call, the middle-aged husband came down from upstairs.
“Mind if I turn on the TV?”
he asked casually.
“Not at all.{r}{p}Go ahead.”
When I answered, he turned on the TV with the remote on the table.
Seeing some trivial drama on, he
flipped through the channels one after another.
“Nothin'.
Nothin' on anywhere.{r}{p}Guess I gotta wait a bit.”
He turned off the TV and faced us.
“You kids happen to know today's closing prices?”
“Huh?
Clos...ing what?”
“Stock prices, stock prices.
This is the middle of nowhere, so there's no evening paper.{r}{p}Shoulda brought a radio.”
“Mr. Kayama, you promised to forget about work.”
Mr. Kobayashi called to him.
“Ah, Kobayashi.
...No, it ain't work.{r}{p}I just check 'em every day, so I feel funny if I don't.”

“What about your wife?{r}{p}Since you married, it's been work, work, work, and you've never taken a trip.{r}{p}Maybe, for once, a trip just the two of you would be nice...{r}{p}Wasn't that you who said so, Mr. Kayama?”
Having said that much, Mr. Kobayashi noticed we were watching and cut himself off.
“Ah, let me introduce you.{r}{p}Mr. Kayama, this is my niece, {n2}.{r}{p}And this is {n1}, who may become my nephew-in-law.”
Nephew-in-law
“Oh, Uncle.
Don't decide things on your own.”
Please, decide away.
“Is that so?
Your niece, huh?{r}{p}Mighty pretty for a niece of yers.”
He looked {n2} over with a leering gaze.
Or maybe I was imagining it.
“Mr. Kayama helped me a great deal back when I was in my old line of work.{r}{p}He's a company president in Osaka.”
“Hello.”
“Pleased to meet you.”
“Still, ain't this somethin'?
Mighty fine inn, ain't it?{r}{p}I've known guys who quit the salaryman life to start udon or soba {C3}(Japanese noodles){C0} shops, but I ain't never seen one run this solid...
.{r}{p}You kids students?”
Mr. Kayama looked our way.
“Y-yes...”
“Take a lesson from yer uncle.
This man's a great one.{r}{p}By the way, you...
got a job lined up yet?”
“No,
not yet...”
“Not yet, huh?
Then come work for me.{r}{p}My company's great, I tell ya.
We go by ability. A second-year employee can make more than a tenth-year, no problem.”
He rattled it off at the top of his voice.
“Well,
but...”
“On the flip side, those with no ability never get a raise.{r}{p}...So what d'ya say?
Come work for me.”
I couldn't tell how serious he was.
“That's still a way off, so...”
I gave a safe answer.
But Mr. Kayama didn't seem to be listening.
“They're all squawkin' about a recession these days.{r}{p}Not us. Don't matter.{r}{p}'Cause we only hire folks with ability.{r}{p}We're a meritocracy.
So how 'bout it, come on over?”
Mr. Kobayashi and {n2} just watched, grinning.
well... I'll think about it.”
I wanted to end this topic somehow.
“Now, why's my company so strong in a recession?
Well, y'see...”
It didn't look like he'd stop anytime soon.
“You're being a nuisance.
dear.”
A quiet woman's voice spoke.
I turned and saw the pretty woman, apparently Mrs. Kayama, standing at the foot of the stairs.
“You're making them uncomfortable.”
From a distance they had seemed mismatched, but up close I could tell she was younger than I'd thought.
She looked thirty-five or so, a gap of at least ten years from Mr. Kayama, even at a conservative guess.
“That's my wife, Haruko.
...And this here's Kobayashi's niece and her fiancé, so I hear.”
Facts on the ground were steadily being established.
{n2} seemed to have lost the will to object.
“Hello.”
“Nice to meet you.”
Haruko smiled warmly and sat down next to Mr. Kayama.
“It was a lovely dinner.”
“You're not just flattering me, are you?”
Even as he said so, Mr. Kobayashi looked far from displeased.
“Flattery? Not at all.{r}{p}It was truly wonderful.”
“Hearing that from you, ma'am, gives me confidence.”
A strangely intimate air filled the room.
“Could I get a beer?”
Mr. Kayama said irritably.
“Of course.
And would you two like some?”
Mr. Kobayashi smoothed it over.
{n2} and I nodded.
“Then,
just a little.”
She showed the amount with her fingers, so I...
“A little.”
I said modestly.
Mr. Kobayashi disappeared into the kitchen at the back of the dining room.
Suddenly something heavy thudded outside the window.
“Whoa.
Something... fell.”
When I jumped, {n2} giggled.
“Just snow sliding off the roof.”
“Oh, snow.”
I felt let down.
Was it really snow?
As I stared doubtfully into the darkness outside, I noticed a light flickering faintly in the distance.
Headlights.
They approached rapidly, and I could hear the engine too.
There were no other houses nearby, so it had to be the late guest.
Sure enough, the engine went around to the back of the inn and cut off there.
Soon footsteps sounded on the entrance porch, and I heard the double doors open
“Excuse me!
Mikimoto here! Anyone around?”
A booming voice carried all the way over to us.
“Mr. Mikimoto, is it?
Welcome.”
Mr. Kobayashi ran out of the dining room.
The big man took off his shoes and stepped up.
Mr. Kobayashi hurriedly set the beer on the table and dashed to the front desk.
“Whew, there was a moment I wondered what would become of me.{r}{p}The wipers were useless and the car got stuck...”
The man called Mikimoto kept talking as he signed in at the front desk.
For someone with a name like that, he had a bearded face and looked every bit the mountain man.
“Dinner is over, but I could prepare something like onigiri {C3}(rice balls){C0}.{r}{p}Shall I make you some?”
Mr. Kobayashi asked.
no, I snacked a lot on the way, so I'm not hungry.{r}{p}Something warm to drink would be nice, though...”
“Would you like coffee or tea or something?{r}{p}We can do soup too, if you like.”
“Then tea, please.”
“Shall I bring it to your room?{r}{p}Or in the lounge over there...?”
“Oh, there's fine.”
Mr. Mikimoto glanced our way and nodded.
“All right.
Here's your key.{r}{p}Come back down after you drop off your luggage.”
Handed the key by Mr. Kobayashi, Mr. Mikimoto shouldered his bags and went up to the second floor.
The cuckoo clock chimed once.
Eight-thirty.
“Oh, sorry.
Go ahead and drink without me.”
Mr. Kobayashi called to us and went back to the dining room.
“Well then, I'll take ya up on that and drink first.”
Mr. Kayama, I, and {n2} picked up our glasses.
“Cheers!”
We struck a light toast pose and took a sip.
Mr. Kayama's wife...
Haruko, either couldn't drink or didn't want to, and didn't reach for one.
“Ahh!
Warmin' up the room on a cold night like this and drinkin' a cold beer is the greatest luxury there is.{r}{p}Don'tcha think?”
Mr. Kayama was beaming.
“I do.”
I agreed.
Indeed, beer in a room heated almost too warm, watching the blizzard, had a different taste from midsummer beer.
“Good evening, everyone!”
With loud footsteps, Mr. Mikimoto, who had just gone up, came back down.
“Oh, you folks are on beer?{r}{p}Just my luck.
And here's a man nearly frozen to death.”
He seemed an awfully cheerful man, laughing loudly as he sat down next to {n2}.
“Oh, Mr. Mikimoto.
You're already down?{r}{p}Your tea's being made now...”
Mr. Kobayashi came back with more beer.
True to his word, his wife Kyoko and the part-timer Midori arrived carrying a tray with a teapot and cups.
“Haruko, beer's not for you, right?
How about tea?{r}{p}We also have something called Mississippi mud cake...
it's delicious.”
When Kyoko asked, Haruko thought for a moment and nodded.
“Yes.
Then I'll have some.”
“Ah,
I feel alive again!”
Mr. Mikimoto drank his piping hot tea gratefully, blowing on it.
With bearded people it's hard to tell their age, and Mr. Mikimoto was no exception.
From his voice and way of talking, he wasn't quite middle-aged yet, probably mid-thirties.
Without the beard he might turn out to be about our age, barely twenty or so.
“Is this everyone staying here?”
Having caught his breath, Mr. Mikimoto looked around at us and asked.
“No,
there are about four more guests.”
Mr. Kobayashi answered.
“That's right.{r}{p}Midori.
They might want tea too.{r}{p}Go ask them, would you?”
“Okay!”
Midori pattered off in her slippers toward the front desk.
“Um, what about the man? The kind of scary-looking one...”
She turned back to us and asked.
She must have meant the yakuza-looking man.
“Oh, Mr. Tanaka.
Ask him anyway.”
“Huh?
...I don't want to.”
“If you don't want to, never mind.
He didn't seem the sociable type anyway.”
“Phew.”
Midori called the three girls on the intercom.
“Boss!
They want to drink.{r}{p}They're coming over now!”
She hung up and shouted toward us.
“If only she could use more polite language...”
Mr. Kobayashi muttered with a wry smile.
I said nothing.
“Then I'll prepare three more for them.”
Kyoko took the tray and disappeared into the kitchen.
“Wow,
the service here is incredible.”
Mr. Mikimoto shook his head in admiration.
“Well, I started this because I love hosting people, after all...”
Mr. Kobayashi was bashfully scratching his head.
The trio came down right away.
“Good evening!”
“Hey, Kanako.{r}{p}Quit pushing.”
“I still wanted to watch TV...”
It got noisy in no time.
“Wow,
smells good!”
“Excuse me, coming through!”
“I said, Kanako.{r}{p}Quit pushing!”
With more people, we decided to sit on the stairs.
Even so, the sofas were packed.
Almost at the same moment, Kyoko brought the tea.
“I asked Toshio too, but
he's watching TV and says he doesn't want any now.”
“Thanks for the tea!”
